answer.rationale: Primary expires in 14 days with no auto-renew while the line sits at 94% and no buffer, so the single decision must keep continuity. Mid-cycle they refused to reopen price, but c4 is specifically about leverage at renewal and c6 about volume/term structure with the same incumbent cutting unit cost without a cutover; that is the only path that can lower TCO without raising delivery risk. c1 argues against a supplier change: integration and scheduled deliveries stayed intact only when we stayed put. Switching on c2 would be a hard cutover into a no-buffer line and therefore increases delivery risk. Adding a second source (c3) does not replace the expiring primary and cannot be paired with a renewal this cycle. Deferring (c5) does not apply: that case was non-critical and continued month-to-month; this contract dies. Scale stays below a multi-year broad lock-in until the archive confirms how c4/c6 actually moved price. Negotiation failure still leaves a supply cliff, so downstream production value is flagged and the 18% outcome is not assumed.
